extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers interested in PG&E and California utilities
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article summarizing Pacific Gas & Electric Company's history, incidents, regulatory actions, liabilities, and generation portfolio. Meant to inform readers about PG&E's operations, legal exposures, and environmental issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation and verification (Wikipedia editorial requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: This section needs additional citations for verification. Please help improve this article by adding citations to reliable sources in this section. Unsourced material may be challenged and removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit Wikipedia editorial guidance: add reliable sources (news, newspapers, books, scholar, JSTOR). Unsourced material may be challenged and removed. The page contains multiple 'needs additional citations' and 'needs update' notices; editors should find and add verifiable references for claims (e.g., generation portfolio numbers, incident causes, remediation timelines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse condemnation (wildfire liability standard in California)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state's constitution enshrined a principle of 'inverse condemnation' for wildfire liability, which means that utilities are held responsible for damages resulting from any fire caused by their equipment, even if their maintenance on equipment and surrounding vegetation was done to standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: California's application of inverse condemnation is described as unique (normally applied to government entities). Under this interpretation utilities can be held liable regardless of compliance with regulatory standards; the page notes this policy resulted in approximately $30 billion of liability for PG&E from the 2017 & 2018 fires and contributed to its bankruptcy. Use this principle when assessing utility liability exposure in California wildfire cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual wildfire prevention plan and PSPS-related regulatory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilities (including PG&E) are required to submit an annual wildfire prevention plan to state regulators. The California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) and related reviewers suggested adding more metrics and maintenance partnerships with local governments, and recommended investigating technical measures (e.g., disabling equipment that restarts power transmission) to reduce need for Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CPUC Resolution ESRB-8 (July 2018) supported use of de-energization and established notification, mitigation, and reporting requirements for PSPS. Reviewers recommended concrete metrics and partnerships; utilities may petition to amend deadlines. When preparing or evaluating a wildfire prevention plan, include measurable metrics, maintenance partnerships, notification plans, mitigation steps, and consider technical mitigations to reduce PSPS reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: PSPS execution and communication expectations (enforcement consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public Safety Power Shutoffs (PSPS) must be executed with appropriate notification, mitigation, and reporting; failure to adequately communicate PSPS actions can lead to enforcement and fines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites CPUC guidance and enforcement actions: in 2021 California fined PG&E $106 million for insufficient communication during 2019 PSPS executions. Best practice/expectation: provide timely, clear public notifications, mitigation plans for vulnerable customers, robust reporting to regulators, and continuous improvement (e.g., use predictive models) to minimize unnecessary outages and regulatory penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wildfire trust fund and changed liability threshold (policy reform)
rubrics_metrics.description: A $21 billion wildfire trust fund was created in July 2019 to pay for damages from future wildfires, seeded 50-50 by utility and customer monies, and the reform reduced the liability threshold so that customers must prove negligence before utilities are held liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy change alters post-fire compensation pathways and the standard of proof for liability—shifting some costs to a trust fund and raising the evidentiary burden for plaintiffs. Use knowledge of the trust fund structure and the negligence threshold when assessing likely recoveries, litigation strategies, and utility financial exposure.
